newsitem.title: UK: Full text of October UK purchasing managers survey.
newsitem.headline: Full text of October UK purchasing managers survey.

text.p: Following is the full text of the October Report on Business (Purchasing Managers' Survey) of the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and (CIPS).
MANUFACTURING ECONOMY SEES FIFTH CONSECUTIVE MONTH OF ACCELERATING GROWTH
The Purchasing Managers' Index rose to an eighteen month high in October and indicated an increase in the rate of expansion within the manufacturing sector for the fifth consecutive month.

Manufacturing output growth slowed gradually between mid-1994 and the middle of this year, since when it has risen steadily. This recent phase of growth in output prompted firms to increase employment in October. This was the first significant increase in manufacturing recruitment since March last year.

The latest rise in output was driven by an increase in the rate of growth of new orders. This was the fifth successive monthly improvement in order books and, as in recent months, orders for consumer goods showed the greatest increase.

However, the survey also found demand to have spread more evenly across manufacturing in October, with stronger demand for investment goods leading to the sharpest increase in output of capital goods seen since February 1995.

Demand for intermediate goods (components) registered somewhat slower growth than demand for finished goods. This largely reflected policies of stock reduction: the amount of goods purchased by manufacturers showed only modest growth, despite the strong growth of output, as existing stocks were used up in production.

Purchasing managers have been able to run stocks at lower, more efficient, levels because both the availability of inputs has been good and the prices of these purchases have been falling over the past year. In October, just under a fifth of all companies reported a further drop in average prices paid for materials while only around 7% saw prices rise. The Prices Index signalled a fall in overall prices as a result.

However, tentative signs of a tightening of price and supply conditions emerged in the October survey. First, the Prices Index, although still signalling falling prices, also registered a falling rate of decline for the third month running. Second, suppliers' delivery times showed the first lengthening in over a year.

The increase in demand for goods from purchasing managers in recent months, although modest, was reported to have been sufficient to put pressure on some suppliers' capacity. With supply for some goods having tightened, firms have reported less success in negotiating discounts.
The Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) is a composite indicator designed to provide an overall view of activity in the manufacturing economy and acts as a leading indicator for the whole economy.

The indicator is derived from individual diffusion indices which measure changes in output, new orders, employment, suppliers' delivery times and stocks of goods purchased. A reading of the PMI below 50% indicates that the manufacturing economy is generally declining; above 50%, that it is generally expanding.
The seasonally adjusted index may be subject to revision as improved estimation of seasonal adjustments occur with each month's new data.
OUTPUT

The seasonally adjusted Output Index recorded strong growth again in October, albeit lower than in the previous month. The slowdown in manufacturing output bottomed out in May and production has now risen in each of the past five months. As in recent months, the consumer sector recorded the sharpest rise during October, but production of investment and intermediate goods also showed significant gains.
NEW ORDERS

The seasonally adjusted New Orders Index rose to its highest level since September 1994. In addition to the strong growth in demand for consumer goods, orders for capital goods rose markedly in October. The weakest growth in demand was recorded by producers of intermediate goods, reflecting the continued desire for firms to deplete stock levels. Export orders continued to rise, but to a lesser extent than UK orders.
QUANTITY OF PURCHASES

The Quantity of Purchases Index remained above 50.0 and therefore indicated a rise in the amount of goods purchased in October. The fall in the index reflects a decline in the rate of growth compared with the previous month, to a level significantly below the current rate of growth of output. This was attributed to the need to reduce stock holdings of inputs and raw materials for cost considerations.
PRICES

The seasonally adjusted Prices Index indicated falling prices for the 12th consecutive month and remained at a historically low level as world-wide demand remained relatively weak compared with supply. Supply was reported to have tightened for selected inputs, however, allowing suppliers of certain goods to raise prices.
SUPPLIERS' DELIVERY TIMES

The seasonally adjusted Delivery Times Index fell below 50.0 and thereby signalled the first overall lengthening of manufacturers' lead-times since September 1995. Increased demand for goods has meant that suppliers have become busier. However, over 90% of all companies reported no problems with suppliers having been unable to meet order levels without incurring delays.
STOCKS OF PURCHASES

The seasonally adjusted Stocks of Purchases Index fell to its lowest level (indicating the largest monthly fall) since December 1992 as stocks fell in over a quarter of all firms. The fall could be largely attributed to destocking policies. On average, fewer inputs were bought than were required for the month's production in a deliberate effort to reduce stock levels and thereby improve cash flow.
STOCKS OF FINISHED GOODS

Stocks of finished goods dropped in over a quarter of all companies during October, leading to an overall decline in stock holdings. The fall generally reflected ongoing stock reduction exercises in order to improve efficiency. However, the size of the fall also reflected the strength of sales of consumer, investment and intermediate goods during the month.
EMPLOYMENT

The seasonally adjusted Employment Index rose to its highest level since March 1995, signalling a modest increase in recruitment during October. The recruitment was generally explained by the need to increase capacity in the light of strengthening order book growth. The expansion was most marked in the consumer goods sector, where firms have seen the sharpest increase in demand in recent months.
CONSUMER GOODS

The consumer goods sector continued to record the strongest growth in order levels as it has done in every month so far this year. The strength of demand prompted both a further acceleration in the rate of growth of output and an increase in employment in order to boost capacity to meet future order book growth.

Higher output necessitated a sharp rise in the quantity of goods purchased, but delivery times lengthened as suppliers were increasingly unable to meet this growth in producers' requirements. On the whole prices paid for these inputs fell again, but the tightening of demand allowed some suppliers to raise prices. As a result, the fall in prices was the smallest recorded since last December.
INVESTMENT/CAPITAL GOODS

Having shown little growth since August last year, manufacturers of investment (capital) goods reported a significant improvement in orders from both domestic and overseas markets for the second month running in October. This led to the largest monthly increase in production since February 1995 and a modest increase in employment. The quantity of goods purchased showed only a modest rise compared with the growth of output and orders, however, as firms ran down high levels of stocks of purchases. This weakness of demand for materials was reflected in both suppliers' delivery times and prices: prices showed the sharpest monthly fall yet recorded by this sector, while deliveries times were largely unchanged.
INTERMEDIATE GOODS

New orders for intermediate goods (components) rose for the fifth month running in October. The UK market continued to provide the main source of growth with demand from export markets remaining subdued in comparison. Output also rose for the fifth consecutive month, albeit to a slightly lesser extent than in September, as capacity was increased through the first significant rise in employment in this sector so far this year. Output growth continued to be restricted by high levels of unsold stock, however, while similarly high stocks of raw materials led to a drop in the quantity of goods purchased. Prices of purchases fell on average again as a result, but the Prices Index rose to its highest level since last December.
